item.title: Exposition
item.description:
Exposition: Student Lecture Notes

Resources

  • Resource 1 — Illustration:. Link to Resource 1
  • Resource 2 — Comparison and Contrast:. Link to Resource 2
  • Resource 3 — Cause and Effect:.Link to Resource 3

1. What is Exposition?

  • Definition: Writing that explains/gives information (not persuasive). Answers:
    • How something works
    • How something happens
    • What the outcome may be
    • Why a situation exists
  • Common Development Methods (often combined):
    Illustration (examples), comparison & contrast, cause & effect, classification, definition, process analysis

2. Core Traits of Good Expository Essays

  1. Significant: Useful info + personal insight (not just data lists).
  2. Clear:
    • Follow structure: Intro (thesis) → Body → Conclusion
    • Use logical support + exact words (no vague/ornamental language).
  3. Objective: No distorted facts.
  4. Economical: Cut unnecessary words/sentences.
  5. Interesting: Fresh examples (avoid overused ideas).

3. Basic Structure (Essay & Paragraph)

Essay (4–5 Paragraphs)

  • Introduction: Announce topic → background → thesis (last sentence).
  • Body Paragraphs:
    • 1 main point each (topic sentence, usually first).
    • Support with facts, examples, details.
  • Conclusion: Restate thesis/summarize key points → final comment (e.g., prediction, solution).

Paragraph

  • Topic Sentence: General claim (e.g., “Campus clubs build useful skills”).
  • Support: Specific details/examples (e.g., “Debate club practices 5-minute speeches weekly”).

4. Introductions & Thesis Statements

Effective Introductions (Hook → Background → Thesis)

  • Hook (1–2 sentences): Anecdote, quote, statistic, description, definition (no long stories).
  • Bridge: Connect hook to topic (name key noun, e.g., “recorded lectures”).
  • Background (1–2 sentences): Define terms/set scope (e.g., “for first-year courses”).
  • Thesis: Final sentence (clear focus + preview if helpful).

Thesis Statements for Exposition

  • Purpose: Tell readers what you’ll explain and how you’ll organize it.
  • Anatomy:
    Topic + Controlling Idea (focus) + [Optional] Organizational Preview
    Example: “Default lecture recording improves first-year exam prep by providing day-one access and repeatable walkthroughs.”
  • Key Rules:
    • Be specific (name “first-year students,” not just “students”).
    • Use measurable verbs/nouns (e.g., “reduce delays” vs. “good”).
    • Match mode (e.g., “compared with” for contrast; “because” for cause & effect).
    • Avoid empty phrases: “In this essay, I will…” or questions as theses.

Good vs. Weak Thesis Examples

Mode Weak Thesis Strong Thesis
Illustration “Digital textbooks help students.” “For first-year courses, digital textbooks reduce first-week delays via instant delivery and offline access.”
Cause & Effect “Phones hurt learning.” “In large lectures, frequent phone checks reduce focus by splitting attention and breaking note structure.”
Comparison & Contrast “Recorded vs. live classes differ.” “Compared with live-only delivery, default recording improves exam review but preserves less spontaneous Q&A.”

5. Planning an Expository Essay (8 Steps)

  1. Pick a focused topic (manageable scope).
  2. Write a clear thesis.
  3. Choose a primary method (e.g., cause & effect).
  4. Organize main points/support.
  5. Write topic sentences (align with thesis).
  6. Draft body paragraphs (develop each point).
  7. Write introduction (hook → thesis).
  8. Write conclusion (restate → final comment).

6. Expository Method 1: Illustration (Using Examples)

What is Illustration?

Writing that uses examples to support a point (makes abstract ideas concrete).

This week we transition into writing: clear, well-structured paragraphs are the building blocks of effective essays. We draw on three course readings:

item.title: Critical Thinking
item.description:
Critical Thinking (Weeks 1–2)

Use these notes to preview before class and review after class. You’ll see key ideas, quick checkpoints, and short practice tasks.

🎯 Learning Outcomes

By the end of this unit you should be able to:

  • Define critical thinking and name the core intellectual standards: clarity, precision, accuracy, relevance, consistency, logical correctness, completeness, fairness.
  • Explain benefits of critical thinking for decision-making and study.
  • Spot barriers: egocentrism/sociocentrism, unwarranted assumptions & stereotypes, relativistic thinking, wishful thinking.
  • Differentiate warranted vs. unwarranted assumptions and recognize stereotypes as a kind of hasty generalization.
  • Apply a rational-acceptance guide to decide when it is reasonable to accept a premise or claim.

📚 Materials

  • Supplementary Reading: what is critical thinking
  • Exercise: Identifyingn assumptions

1) What is Critical Thinking?

Critical thinking is a set of skills and dispositions for identifying, analyzing, and evaluating arguments and claims; overcoming biases; giving convincing reasons; and making reasonable decisions about what to believe and do.

item.title: 批判性思维与英语写作（二）｜Critical Thinking and English Writing II — Syllabus
item.description:
批判性思维与英语写作（二）

Critical Thinking and English Writing II — Syllabus

Semester Length: 18 weeks · 2 × 45 minutes/week
Credits: 2
Target Students: Third-year English majors Language of Instruction: English (with Chinese scaffolding where useful)
Course Type: Required, foundational

📘 Course Description

This course refines academic writing with a strong focus on argumentation. Students learn to take clear positions, build logical reasoning, integrate credible evidence, address counter-arguments, and avoid fallacies. We also strengthen paragraph writing and exposition as support skills, and engage critically with writing in the age of AI—especially for non-native speakers.

item.title: Course Introduction
item.description:
Welcome to Critical Thinking & English Writing II!
The introduction includes: getting acquainted, previewing the course, and practicing writing + critical thinking from day one.

🎯 Learning Goals

  • Build a supportive class community.
  • Understand course outcomes, assessments, and expectations.
  • Produce a short diagnostic writing sample.

🧭 Lesson Overview

Session A

  1. Getting to know each other and activities
  2. Course overview (highlights from the syllabus)

Session B

  1. Activity B — Text Snapshot Analysis
  2. Diagnostic Writing — Writing, Me, and AI
  3. Wrap-up & next steps

👋 Getting to Know You — Name Tent

Goal: Help the instructor quickly learn names, pronunciations, and memorable facts—without repeating peer intros students already know.
